extracted.intended_audience: scholars and graduate students in philosophy, humor theory, and literary/cultural studies (readers interested in Bergson and the theory of comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of Henri Bergson's account of the comic in Le Rire, situating its criteria within his later metaphysics (Creative Evolution, The Two Sources) and explicating what makes something laughable and what function laughter serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mechanical encrusted on the living
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson’s most famous formulation: we laugh whenever we find 'the mechanical is encrusted [plaqué] on the living.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an image of the laughable (e.g., a fishmonger who can only throw as if it were a fish, a particle physicist who only sees particles). The essay emphasizes this is a result of one path of inquiry, not a full definition of the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic concerns only the human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic, Bergson concludes, 'concerns only the human.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughable phenomena are tied to human ways of attention, social roles, and flexible adaptation; examples in Laughter include stage scenes and everyday human slips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / appeal to pure intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is 'accompanied by an “absence of feeling”' and 'appeals exclusively to “pure intelligence.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic effect is intellectual rather than emotional; pity or strong emotion are not features of what we laugh at (this distinguishes the laughable from pathos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter requires an echo (a community)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter 'requires an echo: that is, it requires a community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions socially — it presupposes an audience and operates as a social corrective; solitary occurrences are not the full phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughable arises from social rigidity / suspension of teleodynamic flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable emerges when a society's teleodynamic activity—its flexible evolution of norms—is placed in abeyance; society demands 'tension and elasticity' and laughs at those who show 'a growing callousness [le raidissement] to social life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughable behavior is that which displays rigidity or failure to adapt to present social expectations; laughter serves to chastise and return the individual to social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily rigidity is laughable because it reverses 'the properly human dominance of form over matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid postures or behaviors make the human actor resemble a mechanism rather than a living being; these examples are prominent in Bergson's treatment of physical comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetitive bodily actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of bodily actions causes the human to resemble a mechanism and thus provoke laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series of repeated incidents (e.g., repetitive gestures) exemplify mechanization of life and are a method of 'light comedy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Outward characteristics of the living vs. mechanical (methods of light comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson contrasts three outward characteristics of the living with counterparts of the mechanical: living = continual change of aspect; irreversibility of the order of phenomena; individuality of a perfectly self-contained series. Mechanical = repetition; inversion; reciprocal interference of series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each mechanical counterpart corresponds to comic devices used in theater (repetition, role-reversal/inversion like 'the robber robbed,' and reciprocal interference as in mistaken-identity plots). Bergson claims these 'methods of light comedy' exhaust possible methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement that gives illusion of life + impression of mechanical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any arrangement of acts and events is comic which 'gives us, in a single combination, the illusion of life and the distinct impression of a mechanical arrangement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by children's games (jack-in-the-box, dancing-jack, snow-ball) and their magnified dramatic analogues; the comic juxtaposes apparent life-continuity with detectable mechanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language is laughable when it adheres to the three-part criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Language becomes laughable insofar as it exhibits the same three-part features (human, appeals to intelligence, social) and mechanisms of mechanization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson treats laughable effects in words as a minor but analogous domain: linguistic jokes or slips count as comic when they present mechanical relations in human language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic character = unsociability / absentmindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is 'ridiculous' only through some mental attribute resembling 'absent-mindedness'; inattention is 'equivalent to what we have called unsociability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The laughable character displays a 'systematic absentmindedness' that distances them from the practical, social orientation of others (e.g., Don Quixote as exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for rendering comic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Three characteristics by which a comic character can be rendered: (1) the character must be unsociable (not immoral), (2) the spectator’s attention must be drawn to the character’s unintentional and automatic gestures rather than deliberate actions, and (3) the character is marked by automatism—'involuntary gestures' or 'unconscious remarks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination (systematic absentmindedness) produces the most laughable spectacle; examples include theatrical caricature and professional callousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic aims to depict widespread social types for curative effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The comical aims to depict character types 'that are as widespread in a society as possible, thereby achieving a maximum curative effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy's social function is corrective: by portraying common rigidities and types, it amplifies and remedies social 'parasites' (rigid traits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity / professional callousness and professional logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity—'an admiration of ourselves based on the admiration we think we are inspiring in others'—is a common precipitate of the laughable; commonly instantiated as 'professional callousness' and rooted in a 'professional logic' awkward for general life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: judges speaking legalese, doctors, religious officials (Tartuffe) whose occupational habits make them rigid and thus laughable; comedy exposes these professional logics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic absurdity as dream-logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson corrects Gautier: 'Comic absurdity is that of dreams.' The logic of the laughable parallels the 'logic of dreams.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of dream-reasonings that provoke laughter: witticisms (plays on words), comic obsessions (a recurring common element), particular crescendos (arithmetical growth to unexpected outcome), and reciprocal interference of two series (as in dreams where one is 'himself, and not himself').

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as corrective yet initially sympathetic / play-inviting
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'laughter is first and foremost a means of correction,' our first impression of the laughable is 'sympathy'—we treat the person as 'a playmate' and have 'an implicit solicitation to join in the game.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter involves a 'movement of relaxation' from the tension of common-sense work; the audience is momentarily invited to share the play before corrective function reasserts itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as vitality (élan vital) and summons to creative change
rubrics_metrics.description: Read in conjunction with Bergson’s later metaphysics, laughter is 'the élan vital’s vital summons,' not merely corrective but 'the demand of life itself' that human beings question obligations and create new forms of life and community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues Bergson ultimately shows laughter valorizes teleodynamic experimentation—by humiliating calcified forms it enables society to experiment and develop new forms (laughter 'performs a useful function by emphasizing the form of their significant undulations').

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy lies midway between art and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy 'lies midway between art and life. It is not disinterested as genuine art is. By organizing laughter, comedy accepts social life as a natural environment, it even obeys an impulse of social life. And in this respect it turns its back upon art, which is a breaking away from society and a return to pure nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy is utilitarian and social (organizes laughter to correct), whereas art seeks a 'more direct vision of reality' and detachment; this situates comic practice functionally between art and social life.
